transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you start by telling me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I'm here because of my husband's sister. She's been... working her way into our family business. I can see exactly what she's doing—she's trying to get control of the money and push me completely out of any decisions. People keep trying to smooth it over and tell me it's fine, but I know what I've been seeing. It's been going on for more than a year now, and I'm just not going to ignore it anymore.
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people around you don't seem to hear or see?

No, I... I don't have anything like that. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. My eyes and ears work just fine, doctor. I just pay attention to what she's actually doing in the real world.
Aside from this situation with your sister-in-law, would you say you've generally had a hard time trusting other people—friends, coworkers, even before this all started?

No, I... I wouldn't say that at all. I've always gotten along just fine with my friends and the people in my neighborhood. I don't go around thinking everybody is out to get me or anything like that. 

I've never really had a hard time trusting people. It's just... well, it's just her. And that's only because I can actually see what she's doing with the business. Before she started all this, everything was perfectly fine.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a single, fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (that her sister-in-law is conspiring to seize control of the family business and exclude her) persisting for over a year. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech, and no other psychotic symptoms, and her functioning and relationships outside this specific belief system remain intact. She explicitly denies pervasive distrust or suspiciousness toward others (ruling out paranoid personality disorder) and denies perceptual disturbances (ruling out schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders with hallucinations). The plausible, circumscribed nature of the belief, its chronicity (>1 month, here >1 year), and preserved psychosocial functioning outside the delusional theme are classic for Delusional Disorder, persecutory/jealous subtype.
